transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Korva Coleman.
Democrats have flipped control of Congress in the midterm elections.
They picked up seven more seats in the Senate with two races yet to be called in Alaska
and Mississippi.
Democrats claimed more than two dozen House seats.
Dozens of races are still uncalled.
One of the Senate seats that was flipped was in South Carolina.
Republican Senator Darlene Graham, sister to late Senator Lindsey Graham, lost to Democrat
and pediatrician Annie Andrews.
Andrews spoke to South Carolina supporters last evening.
You have shown the nation that in this era of partisan divides, of vitriol and name-calling,
in a politics dominated by billionaires and special interest groups and insiders in Washington,
D.C., that we will not bow down.
Other Senate races flipped by Democrats came in North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Kansas
and Texas.
A Democrat picked up the open Michigan Senate seat.
Democrats also did well with gubernatorial races.
In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms will become the nation's first-ever black female governor.
Deb Holland of New Mexico will become the first-ever Native American female governor.
Javier Becerra will govern California, David Crowley will run Wisconsin, Aaron Ford will
lead Nevada, and Gina Inajosa will become the first Latina to govern Texas.
And Bear's Barbara Sprunt reports that congressional Democrats are reviewing a long to-do list.
Control of Congress means control of oversight.
Democrats will act as a check on the White House, which has not been constrained from
the Republican-led Congress thus far.
Democrats are likely to put forward bills to tackle affordability, an issue that propelled
them to victory.
Other areas ripe for action are efforts to reel in data centers and putting guardrails
on A.I.
President Trump has already said he's not afraid to use his veto pen, but he's also
signaled some willingness to work with Democrats and make deals.
Barbara Sprunt, NPR News, Washington.
Stocks opened sharply higher as investors study the election results.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the Dow jumped more than 1,200 points.
The end of GOP rule in Washington could have different effects on different industries
from oil and gas producers to cryptocurrency, but markets generally welcome divided government
as a potential check on excesses by either party.
One loser in Tuesday's election was Elon Musk, who spent more than $400 million packing Republican
candidates.
Stock in both SpaceX and Tesla opened lower.
Both companies are headquartered in Texas, where Democrats won Senate and Governor's
races for the first time in decades.
Cost of living concerns also took a bite out of McDonald's sales, although not as big as
forecasters had expected.
The fast-food giant says customer traffic declined in its most recent quarter.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
You're listening to NPR.
Florida investigators say they've located a piece of the small jet that crashed into
a neighborhood last weekend the fuselage was found miles from the crash site near Palm Beach.
The jet crash killed nine people aboard.
Around the world, adolescents are not getting nearly enough exercise.
That's according to new estimates from the World Health Organization.
NPR's Maria Godoy reports one in four teens said they failed to get at least one hour
of physical activity on any given day in the prior week.
Kids and teens should get at least 60 minutes each day of moderate to vigorous physical
activity like playground play, skateboarding, or soccer, according to public health guidelines.
The WHO says globally just 14 percent of adolescents meet these recommendations.
On average, adolescents reported being active for less than three days a week, a situation
that the WHO says hasn't improved in the last 15 years.
And in almost every country, the report found girls were less likely to be active than boys.
The findings were based on population-based surveys in 140 countries and territories.
They appear in the journal The Lancet Global Health.
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
The central bank in Paraguay has seized a major digital bank with close ties to Paraguayan
President Santiago Pena.
God has thrown hundreds of millions of dollars into limbo belonging to customers and to Paraguayan
public funds.
Paraguayan authorities say the digital bank appears to be failing.
Prosecutors have ordered arrests.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Democrats flip control of Congress in midterms, picking up Senate seats and House seats
Annie Andrews defeats Senator Darlene Graham in South Carolina Senate race
Keisha Lance Bottoms becomes Georgia's first Black female governor; several other governor races won by Democrats
Congressional Democrats plan oversight of White House and bills on affordability, data centers, and AI
Stocks open sharply higher as investors react to election results; Dow jumps over 1,200 points
Elon Musk loses in election after spending over $400 million backing Republicans; SpaceX and Tesla stock open lower
McDonald's reports customer traffic decline in latest quarter amid cost-of-living concerns
Florida investigators locate fuselage of small jet that crashed into neighborhood, killing nine
WHO estimates most adolescents worldwide fail to get recommended daily physical activity
Paraguay's central bank seizes digital bank tied to President Santiago Pena; prosecutors order arrests
